language_wrapper: In a math contest, consider the set of consecutive integers {lower, lower+1, ..., n}. A set has the [gon_sides]-gon property if it contains [gon_sides] distinct elements whose largest is strictly less than the sum of the other [gon_sides]-1 elements (so those [gon_sides] numbers can be the side lengths of a non-degenerate [gon_sides]-gon). Determine the largest integer n such that every [subset_size]-element subset of {lower, lower+1, ..., n} has the [gon_sides]-gon property.
hardness_rationale: The seed asks for triangles (r=3) in 10-element subsets starting at 4 and reduces to a 2-step Fibonacci growth argument. Our family generalizes to r-gons: in every s-element subset, some r elements must form a non-degenerate polygon (largest side less than the sum of the other r-1). Avoiding r-gons forces an (r-1)-step summation recurrence (k-bonacci) with strictly larger combinatorial complexity, requiring extremal sequence arguments and bounding via exponential-type growth in higher dimensions. Handling arbitrary start lower and parameters (r, s) requires deeper insight into the structure of r-gon-free sets and careful reasoning to derive the closed-form threshold.
notes:
Proof of correctness (outline):
1) Definitions. An r-gon (r ≥ 3) can be formed by r positive side lengths if and only if the largest side is strictly less than the sum of the remaining r−1 sides. An s-element subset lacks the r-gon property exactly when every r-element sub-subset fails this, i.e., for any chosen largest element c, the sum of any r−1 smaller elements is ≤ c.
2) Extremal structure. Let a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_s be any increasing r-gon-free sequence. For each i ≥ r, considering c = a_i and the r−1 largest smaller elements (a_{i−1}, ..., a_{i−(r−1)}), we must have a_{i−1} + ... + a_{i−(r−1)} ≤ a_i. This condition is sufficient to guarantee r-gon-freeness because the sum of any r−1 smaller elements is maximized by the r−1 largest ones.
3) Minimality. To minimize the s-th element among r-gon-free sequences drawn from {lower, lower+1, ...}, we take the smallest possible distinct increasing initial segment: a_1 = lower, a_2 = lower+1, ..., a_{r−1} = lower + (r−2), and then enforce equality in the extremal condition: for i ≥ r, set a_i = a_{i−1} + ... + a_{i−(r−1)}. This yields the minimal possible values while maintaining r-gon-freeness.
4) Threshold. Let A_s(lower, r) denote the s-th term of this minimal sequence. If n ≥ A_s(lower, r), then the constructed length-s r-gon-free sequence lies entirely in {lower, ..., n}, so there exists an s-element subset without the r-gon property. Therefore, to force every s-element subset to have the r-gon property, we must have n < A_s(lower, r). Conversely, if n = A_s(lower, r) − 1, no s-element r-gon-free subset can exist: any r-gon-free s-term sequence must have its maximum at least A_s(lower, r) by minimality, which exceeds n.
5) Conclusion. The largest n for which all s-element subsets of {lower, ..., n} have the r-gon property is exactly A_s(lower, r) − 1, where A_s(lower, r) is computed via the (r−1)-step summation recurrence initialized by consecutive terms starting at lower. This reduces the problem to computing that extremal threshold.
Implementation notes: The verifier reconstructs A_s using integer arithmetic and returns A_s − 1. It also enforces non-triviality. The generator samples parameters to keep values in manageable ranges and retries if instances are trivial or too large.
source_question: A set of positive numbers has the $triangle~property$ if it has three distinct elements that are the lengths of the sides of a triangle whose area is positive. Consider sets $\{4, 5, 6, \ldots, n\}$ of consecutive positive integers, all of whose ten-element subsets have the triangle property. What is the largest possible value of $n$ ?
